name: Museum Augmented Reality
description: Museum augmented reality can connect physical displays with digital models and interpretation. An exhibition about Iran’s Chehrābād salt mine in Bochum, Germany, provides a documented example, although the inspected evidence does not establish a currently operating service inside an Iranian museum.

seo.title: Museum Augmented Reality and Iranian Heritage | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore a documented augmented reality exhibition about Iranian archaeology and the evidence still needed to identify operating services in Iran.

content.heading: Connecting an object with its context
content.content:
An archaeological display can separate an object from the place where it was discovered. The augmented reality project developed for the German Mining Museum Bochum addressed that problem through an exhibition about Chehrābād, an Iranian salt mine associated with naturally preserved human remains known as the Salt Men. Its digital interpretation connected a physical mine model with information about discovery locations. This is an example of Iranian heritage interpreted abroad; it is not evidence of an installation operating in Iran. [s1]

The distinction matters for travelers. A documented exhibition can explain what the technology does without establishing where a visitor can use it today. Neither the developer’s project record nor the exhibition website supplies a verified inventory of current AR services in Iranian museums. [s1][s2]

content.heading: The Chehrābād exhibition
content.content:
ArcTron describes an app supplied on loan tablets, with introductory guidance for museum visitors. Scanning a code associated with the printed mine model revealed digital information points positioned at the discovery locations. Selecting them opened further interpretation. A separate installation presented a digital model associated with Salt Man 4 above an image of the preserved body. These were specific interpretive arrangements, rather than a general-purpose travel app. [s1]

The exhibition’s own account places this technology within a wider archaeological narrative about work, death, and research at the mine. It also identifies a graphic novel imagining a miner’s possible final day. That wording establishes an important boundary: a narrative reconstruction is an interpretation, even when it draws on archaeological findings. [s2]

content.heading: Reading digital interpretation critically
content.content:
The exhibition website explicitly discusses the ethical tension involved in displaying human remains and describes giving physical visitors a way to avoid that section. Digital interpretation belongs within the same discussion: a compelling model does not remove the need to explain what is being shown and why. [s2]

For an international reader, the useful questions are therefore concrete. Does the interpretation identify the excavation evidence? Does it distinguish surviving material from reconstructed appearance? Is an imagined personal story labeled as such? The Chehrābād example makes these editorial questions visible, but the inspected project descriptions do not demonstrate learning outcomes or visitor satisfaction. Those outcomes would require separate evaluation. [s1][s2]

content.heading: What remains to be verified in Iran
content.content: Before this page can serve as a practical guide to Iranian museum AR, research must establish named domestic installations, their operating dates, supported languages, equipment requirements, and current visitor access. Historical project documentation should remain useful as a case study, while availability claims need dated confirmation. The evidence currently supports an explanation of one Iran-related exhibition, rather than a directory of bookable experiences. [s1][s2]

name: Virtual Tours
description: Virtual tours offer different ways to explore Iranian heritage, including reconstructed ancient architecture and digitized exhibitions. Getty’s Persepolis Reimagined illustrates why a historical reconstruction should be distinguished from a record of a place’s present condition.

seo.title: Virtual Tours of Iranian Heritage | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand reconstructed Persepolis and online exhibitions about Iranian archaeology, with clear distinctions between evidence and interpretation.

content.heading: What kind of place are you entering?
content.content:
A virtual tour may reconstruct a vanished building or present an exhibition assembled around surviving objects. These formats answer different questions. Getty’s Persepolis Reimagined offers an interpreted ancient setting, while the Death By Salt website introduces a digitized exhibition about Iranian archaeology. Neither should automatically be read as a current visual survey of an Iranian destination. [s1][s2]

For readers unfamiliar with Iran, this distinction helps connect digital experiences with physical geography. Persepolis is an archaeological site whose monumental remains are recognized by UNESCO. A reconstruction can help explain those remains, but its completed spaces should be understood alongside evidence from the surviving site. [s3]

content.heading: Persepolis as an interpreted ancient environment
content.content:
Getty announced Persepolis Reimagined in April 2022. Its described route begins at the Gate of All Nations, then explores major palace spaces, including the Apadana reception hall and Royal Treasury. Interpretation connects architecture with objects and court practices; the experience also incorporates present-day views. Getty credits collaboration among museum specialists, university consultants, and digital production teams. [s1]

UNESCO describes the actual monument as a palace complex built on a terrace combining natural and constructed ground, with architectural inspiration from Mesopotamia. Reading that account alongside a reconstruction helps separate the archaeological setting from the visual choices used to make an ancient environment legible. A beautifully finished digital room is an explanation to examine, rather than proof that every depicted detail is known. [s3]

content.heading: Following an exhibition rather than rebuilding a city
content.content:
Death By Salt provides a contrasting approach. Its website introduces digital exhibition sections about the Chehrābād mine, research across the Iranian Highlands, and a collaborative exhibition on the search for resources. Here, the organizing framework is an exhibition narrative rather than a reconstructed urban landscape. [s2]

This format invites a different reading habit: identify the institutions responsible for the interpretation, follow the relationship between objects and explanatory material, and distinguish the exhibition’s historical presentation from present visitor information. The site contains legacy pandemic guidance, so its practical notices should not be treated as freshly confirmed arrangements. [s2]

content.heading: A companion to further exploration
content.content:
These examples suggest a useful sequence: establish what survives, examine how the digital presentation interprets it, and return to the source institution for context. Getty’s published description and UNESCO’s site account provide complementary starting points for Persepolis. [s1][s3]

The sources inspected here document the projects and their intended content. They do not establish uninterrupted playback, accessibility, or compatibility on every device. A virtual experience can deepen an encounter with Iranian heritage while still leaving practical travel questions—entry, opening arrangements, and current physical access—to separate verification.

name: Attraction Discovery Platforms
description: Attraction discovery platforms organize destinations through searches, categories, and maps. Visit Iran’s tourism interface and UNESCO’s property records illustrate complementary ways to discover places while checking their identity and heritage significance.

seo.title: Attraction Discovery Platforms for Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Learn how tourism categories and authoritative heritage records can help identify Iranian attractions without confusing discovery with verified access.

content.heading: Turning an interest into a destination
content.content:
Discovery begins with a question: a historic building, a landscape, a museum, or a place associated with a cultural tradition. Visit Iran’s English tourism map presents named search and category filters, giving readers several ways to begin. Its visible interface separates attractions from facilities and infrastructure, a useful distinction between the reason for a visit and the services supporting it. [s1]

The existence of a filter establishes how the interface organizes information. It does not establish how complete its records are, whether every result is accurate, or whether a listed place can currently receive visitors. Discovery should therefore lead to further checking rather than end the research process.

content.heading: What a tourism interface makes visible
content.content:
Visit Iran offers historical categories such as museums, bridges, bazaars, houses, and palaces, alongside natural features such as caves, mountains, and wetlands or other landscape categories. It also distinguishes cities and rural destinations and provides filters associated with World Heritage and craft cities. These groupings let a reader move beyond a single famous monument toward a wider set of interests. [s1]

Such categories are an editorial structure, not a ranking of importance. A place appearing under one heading may also matter for another reason. Nor should a facility listing be mistaken for a confirmed reservation or a complete account of accessibility. The inspected interface supports discovery; its underlying results and operational details were not independently audited. [s1]

content.heading: Check whether a name means one place or several
content.content:
Authoritative heritage records can clarify what a search result represents. UNESCO’s Persian Garden entry concerns nine gardens in different provinces, rather than one destination called the Persian Garden. Its description explains shared design principles while recognizing adaptation to different climates. A single heritage label can therefore connect geographically separate places. [s2]

Persepolis provides a different case: UNESCO’s record describes a particular archaeological palace complex and its terrace setting. Comparing these records shows why the underlying entity matters. A monument, a group of components, and a broad cultural category should not be treated as interchangeable map points. [s3]

content.heading: Build a shortlist, then verify it
content.content:
A practical research method is to use broad categories to discover candidates, then read a more specific record to understand the site’s identity and significance. For a garden-related itinerary, the UNESCO description helps explain why related places may share a designation without sharing a location. For Persepolis, the property record establishes the archaeological subject behind the name. [s2][s3]

Neither step alone confirms opening arrangements, transport, ticketing, or present conditions. Those details require separately dated information from the relevant operator or authority. Keeping discovery and practical verification as distinct stages makes a shortlist more useful: each place has both an understood identity and a clear list of travel details still to check.
